title: Joy in practice
hook: piti and sukha: joy belongs on the path
tomorrow: who was the Buddha so glad for that he said it twice?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long view: Sumedha in the mud, choosing a road of many lives and starting it that morning. Mai went back to the kids' class on Sunday.

There's a kind of guilt that shows up when something feels too good: a slow Sunday, a long laugh, as if joy must mean you're slacking. A group of monks once had that worry about a friend. Bhaddiya had been a king. Now he was a monk who sat at the foot of trees in the forest, and again and again he said out loud: oh, what bliss! What bliss! The other monks were sure he was missing his palace and his old royal life. So they went and told the Buddha.
screen: `JOY THAT FEELS LIKE SLACKING.` → `A KING, NOW UNDER A TREE.` → `OH, WHAT BLISS!` → `THE MONKS TELL THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: The Buddha called Bhaddiya and asked: is it true? It was. Why? As king, Bhaddiya said, he had guards inside his rooms and outside, guards in the city and across the countryside, and still he lived afraid, on edge, trusting no one. Now, alone at the root of a tree, he lived without fear, at ease, his mind, the text says, like a wild deer's. That was the bliss. The Buddha didn't scold him. He answered with a short verse about a mind gone past fear and sorrow. Here's the teaching under the story. The suttas name two kinds of gladness on the path. Piti is a lifting joy. Sukha is a calmer ease, happiness at rest. Both arise in the early stages of deep meditation; in the first, the texts say, they are born of seclusion. And piti is one of the seven factors of awakening, right beside mindfulness and energy. So in Buddhist teaching joy isn't a prize for later, and it isn't a slip. It's part of the road. The story itself marks the difference: Bhaddiya's bliss wasn't the palace's pleasures coming back. It was the gladness of having nothing left to guard.
screen: `GUARDS EVERYWHERE, AND STILL AFRAID.` · `UNDER A TREE, LIKE A WILD DEER.` · `PITI, THE LIFT. SUKHA, THE EASE.` · `A FACTOR OF AWAKENING.` · then, large: `JOY BELONGS.`

segments.voice: If there's a cup of water or tea nearby, take one slow sip and follow it all the way: cool or warm, the taste, the swallow. If not, rest your attention in your hands and feel their warmth. When any small gladness turns up during the sit, don't push it away and don't chase it; let it stay like a welcome guest.
Joy in practice: piti, the lift, and sukha, the ease. Part of the path, the suttas say, not a detour from it.
Something to keep: joy belongs, like Bhaddiya's at the root of his tree, with nothing left to fear. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1761 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 36 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: WHO WAS THE BUDDHA SO GLAD FOR THAT HE SAID IT TWICE?`

howItsDone: In meditation teaching, piti (joy) and sukha (ease) are named among the qualities that arise as the mind settles; teachers encourage meditators to know them without clinging, as part of the path.

fork.setup: at a retreat, a friend felt lit up with joy during the sit, then panicked that she'd lost focus. what fits the Bhaddiya story?
options: joy from a settling mind is part of the path; know it without grabbing it.
joy means the mind slid back to pleasure; push it away and refocus.
chase that feeling every sit from now on; joy is the whole point.
fork.reveal: the Buddha didn't scold Bhaddiya. the suttas name piti and sukha as part of deep meditation; the practice is to know them, not cling to them.

original.note: Pali: joy, rapture, one of the seven factors of awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: serious practice should feel grim, and joy is a distraction.
what it means: joy belongs on the path; piti and sukha arise as the mind settles.
what a scholar hears: Udana 2.10's cry of 'what bliss', the first jhana's piti and sukha born of seclusion, and piti as a bojjhanga, a factor of awakening.
guess: gladness that arises as part of the path itself
a prize you earn only after years of sitting
the pleasure of treating yourself after a sit

chat.says: sunday with the kids was SO fun. we laughed through the whole breathing game. is that allowed??
options: yes. joy belongs on the path; the Buddha didn't scold Bhaddiya for 'what bliss.'
careful. those monks were right that joy means slipping back to pleasure.
joy only comes after years of sitting, so you probably weren't focused.
chat.meaning: Bhaddiya's 'what bliss' was the ease of a mind free of fear. The suttas name piti and sukha as parts of the path, not slips.

tie.story: Monks reported Bhaddiya for crying 'what bliss!'; he explained it was the ease of living without fear, and the Buddha didn't scold him.
tie.friend: Mai's laughing breathing game with the kids can be real practice, not a failure of focus.
tie.you: where did a small joy show up in your week?

notes: Shape: senses (the sip, the warmth of the hands; Bhaddiya under the tree). Mai's storyline: back at the kids' class on Sunday after telling the truth; the kids laughed through a breathing game, and she wonders if joy is allowed.

Udana 2.10 paraphrased: Bhaddiya, son of Kaligodha, a former ruler, exclaims 'aho sukham' at the foot of a tree and in empty dwellings; monks think he is recalling royal pleasures and report him; he explains guards inside and outside the palace, city and countryside, yet fear; now he lives unafraid, 'with a mind like a wild deer'; the Buddha speaks an inspired verse. Confirm the summary and the verse paraphrase ('a mind gone past fear and sorrow').
First jhana formula (piti and sukha born of seclusion) as in DN 2 and many suttas; seven factors of awakening per SN 46 (the count is the text's). Confirm.
'Sometimes felt as lightness or tingling in the body': common meditation teaching about piti, not from the cited texts; confirm or cut.
Surprising fact: monks once reported a fellow monk to the Buddha for saying 'what bliss', and the Buddha sided with him.
